the National Health Act in South Africa, which was implemented on March 1st 2012, mandates active consent from parents or legal guardians for all research conducted in the health field with participants aged under 18 years; this law may have the unintended effect of reducing participation rates and excluding the most at risk students in school-based sexual and reproductive health studies; and the Act may compromise adolescents' right of dignity and privacy, given that the research is personal in nature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) What are the implications of section 71 of the Act for school-based sexual and reproductive health (SRH) research in South Africa?;
how the National Health Act's provisions for informed consent in school-based adolescent research may compromise the rights to dignity and privacy of the adolescents involved.

the following: (1) whether the National Health Act's consent provisions are consistent with the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki, (2) whether the Act's consent provisions adequately protect the rights and interests of adolescents, (3) whether the Act provides a sufficient balance between the rights of adolescents, parents and researchers, (4) whether the Act adequately addresses the unique needs of adolescents and (5) how the Act's consent requirements may be modified to better serve the needs of adolescents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

section 71's guidelines relating to informed parental consent in the National health Act, No 62, 2003 are not suitable to the needs of adolescents and their right to dignity and participation in research.

, in the context of school-based sexual and reproductive health (SRH) research, the National Health Act's requirement for active consent from a legal guardian is an obstacle to research and should be amended.
the Act is a positive step in protecting research participants, but the Act needs further clarification in order to protect the dignity, privacy and well-being of South African adolescents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have to re-examine the ethical guidelines relating to consent in the National Act in order to better the interests of South Africans in sexual and reproductive research.
the law is not a barrier to the implementation of adolescent health programmes.
the Act should be amended to permit a wider scope of ethical decision-making, including passive consent for school-based research on sexual and reproductive health.
The main takeaway from our work is that

adolescents should be afforded the opportunity to participate in research on issues that directly affect them, while at the same time ensuring that their rights to dignity, privacy and autonomy are upheld.

, in order to ensure that research on adolescent sexual and reproductive issues is inclusive and meaningful to adolescents, the law needs to be amended so that it is not only protective but also empowering to young people.

, while the law is well intentioned, it may have the unintended consequences of compromising the dignity of the most at-risk adolescents, thereby excluding them from research that could benefit their sexual and reproductive well-being.
